references.text: The children ask about the meaning of the Passover celebration, and parents are to explain how the Lord spared the houses of Israel in Egypt.
A parallel command to explain to your son what the Lord's mighty hand did when He brought the people out of Egypt.
A reminder to teach children and grandchildren about what they saw at Horeb, part of the tradition of passing faith to the next generation.
When a son asks about the meaning of the commandments, the father is to tell him about slavery in Egypt and how the Lord brought them out.
The command to impress God's words upon children and speak of them at home and away.
Fathers are to tell the coming generation about the Lord's great works, so that children may put their trust in God.
The purpose of the plagues was for the Israelites to tell their children and grandchildren about the Lord's deeds in Egypt.
The stones from the Jordan are to be a sign, and children are to hear how Israel crossed the Jordan.
These verses form a continuous liturgical unit where 13:8 gives the command to tell, and 13:14 provides the actual answer to give when children ask.
This is the direct parallel to 13:8 in Deuteronomy, where Moses repeats the same liturgical response that is to be given to children.
Both verses use the memory of the Exodus as the theological basis for performing a specific command today.
The verse shows the prophecy of the Exodus, which later becomes the subject of the liturgical telling in 13:8.
Both verses recognize the Exodus from Egypt as the decisive moment when God's covenant relationship with the people was established.
The verses share the same reference to the Exodus as the decisive moment for the making of the covenant, but with different emphasis (teaching versus warning).
Both verses use the memory of the Exodus as the direct basis for performing a specific command about justice.
The verse confirms the theological core of 13:8: that God's identity is inseparably linked to the action He performed at the Exodus.
